value.overview: The Common Yellowthroat is a small, active New World warbler associated with dense, low vegetation near water. Males are recognizable by their bright yellow throat and bold black facial mask bordered in white; females are browner and lack the mask. It breeds widely across North America and many northern populations migrate south for winter. In Costa Rica, it is a relatively uncommon visitor compared with resident yellowthroat species, occurring mainly during migration and the northern winter.
value.classification: The Common Yellowthroat belongs to the order Passeriformes and the family Parulidae, the New World warblers. Its scientific name is Geothlypis trichas.
value.identification: This compact warbler has an olive-brown back, yellow to yellowish underparts, and a relatively short tail. Adult males have a distinctive black mask extending across the eyes and forehead, usually edged above with white, plus a yellow throat and breast. Females are duller, mostly brown and olive, with a pale eye ring or eyebrow and variable yellow on the throat. It often keeps low in vegetation and may be detected first by its repeated, husky witchety-witchety-witchety song.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds from Alaska and southern Canada through most of the United States and into Mexico. It winters from the southern United States through Central America and the Caribbean. In Costa Rica, the Common Yellowthroat is not a regular breeding resident; it occurs mainly as an uncommon winter visitor and passage migrant, especially in suitable lowland and middle-elevation wetlands, marsh margins, reedbeds, ponds, damp thickets, brushy fields, and other dense vegetation near water. Records are generally local and seasonal rather than widespread.
value.migrationStatus: Mostly migratory. In Costa Rica, it is chiefly a passage migrant in roughly October-November and April-early May, with some individuals remaining as uncommon winter residents; it does not normally breed there.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in marshes, wet meadows, wet thickets, brushy fields, overgrown pastures, and other habitats with dense vegetation close to the ground. The female usually builds a small open-cup nest low in grasses, sedges, or shrubs, often near water. Clutches commonly contain three to five eggs. Both adults feed the young, and pairs may raise more than one brood during a breeding season when habitat and food conditions are favorable.
value.dietFeeding: Common Yellowthroats feed mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, including beetles, bugs, caterpillars, grasshoppers, flies, and spiders. They forage low in dense vegetation, moving deliberately through grasses, reeds, and shrubs while gleaning prey from leaves and stems. They may also make short sallies or briefly search on the ground. Small fruits and seeds can be taken occasionally, particularly when insect prey is less available.
value.behavior: This species is secretive but vocal, usually remaining close to the ground and slipping through tangled vegetation rather than flying in the open. Males sing persistently from concealed perches during the breeding season and defend small territories. Common Yellowthroats often flick through reeds and shrubs with quick, nervous movements. During migration and winter, they are usually solitary or found singly, although several may use the same suitable wetland or brushy area.

conservation.populationTrend: The North American population has shown a long-term decline, estimated at approximately 26% from 1966 to 2019, despite the species remaining common overall.
conservation.threats: The principal concerns are loss and degradation of wetlands, marsh edges, wet grasslands, and dense low brush caused by drainage, agricultural conversion, development, and intensive vegetation management. Poor water quality, pesticides, and other pollutants may also reduce insect prey and affect birds using wet habitats. These pressures are relevant to migratory and wintering birds in Costa Rica as well as to breeding populations farther north.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore wetlands, reedbeds, wet grasslands, and brushy stream or pond margins. Retain dense native vegetation and avoid unnecessary clearing during migration and winter. Reducing pesticide use, improving water quality, and supporting protected areas and responsible habitat management can benefit Common Yellowthroats and other wetland-dependent birds.
